Even successful compilers like GCC are hard to reuse because they are architecturally
monolithic, rely heavily on global state, and violate clean layering boundaries—making
them unsuitable as embeddable libraries or JIT infrastructure despite their power.
GCC cannot be reused as libraries,

and diagnosing errors in the input code.
-->then translating the parsed code into LLVM IR (usually, but not always, by

—>LLVM is that it is designed as a set of libraries, rather than as a monolithic
command line compiler like GCC or an opaque virtual machine like the JVM or .NET
—> LLVM is an infrastructure, a collection of useful compiler technology that
can be brought to bear on specific problems (like building a C compiler, or an
optimizer in a special effects pipeline).
—> Instead of one huge optimization algorithm, LLVM uses many small optimizations called passes.
—> Each pass performs one specific kind of optimization
—>Each LLVM pass is written as a C++ class that derives (indirectly) from the Pass class.
—>LLVM optimizer provides dozens of different passes, each of which are written in a similar style.
These passes are compiled into one or more .o files, which are then built into a series of archive libraries (.a files on Unix systems).
—>passes are as loosely coupled as possible
—>explicitly declare their dependencies among other passes if they depend on some other analysis to do their job.
LLVM PassManager uses the explicit dependency information to satisfy these dependencies and optimize the execution of passes.
—>implementer is free to implement their own language-specific passes to cover for deficiencies in the LLVM optimizer or to explicit
The LLVM code generator is responsible for transforming LLVM IR into target specific machine code.
—>Similar to the approach in the optimizer, LLVM's code generator splits the code generation problem
into individual passes—instruction selection, register allocation, scheduling, code layout optimization,
and assembly emission—and provides many builtin passes that are run by default.
—> The target author is then given the opportunity to choose among the default passes, override the defaults and implement
completely custom target-specific passes as required.
—>This flexibility allows target authors to produce great code without having to write an entire code generator from scratch for their target.

LLVM's textual IR lets developers create small, precise unit tests for
individual optimization passes. Instead of compiling an entire C program
and hoping the desired optimization is reached, LLVM can load IR
directly, run one specific pass (using opt), and verify the result (using
FileCheck). This makes regression testing and feature testing much more
you are testing only the thing you care
When LLVM encounters a bug, developers need a small test case that reproduces the problem
and helps identify the faulty component. Manually reducing large test cases is tedious, especially
for bugs that produce incorrect code instead of crashes.
BugPoint is an LLVM tool that automates this process. Given an LLVM IR file and a sequence of optimization passes that trigger a bug, it:
—>Minimizes the input program to the smallest test case that still reproduces the bug.
—> Identifies the optimization pass or code generator responsible.
—> Produces the reduced test case and the command needed to reproduce the failure.
—> LLVM prioritizes rapid improvement over strict backward compatibility.
—> A major future goal is to make LLVM even more modular. Some parts,
especially the code generator, are still too monolithic
—> LLVM's success comes largely from its reusability. Projects can reuse existing
LLVM components instead of building them from scratch. For example, the debugger LLDB reuses
Clang parsers, LLVM's JIT compiler, disassemblers, and target support.
—> The authors believe LLVM can stay successful by:
—> Redesigning or replacing code when necessary.
